mainTopic: Why the Sages forbade wool ציצית on a linen garment even though the הלכה follows בית הלל
overview: A ברייתא records that בית שמאי exempt a linen garment from ציצית and בית הלל obligate it, and the הלכה follows בית הלל. Yet in ירושלים, anyone who put wool תכלת on linen was looked at as strange, and רבי explains that the Sages forbade it because people are not experts in the law. The גמרא tries ways to teach the law instead: ten people wearing it in the market, or a public lecture. Neither works, and the ban is then explained as a גזירה because of קלא אילן, a fake blue dye that would leave a person wearing כלאים with no מצוה. The גמרא asks why fake-blue strings shouldn't at least count as white. It answers that white strings can be made of linen, following ריש לקיש's rule that a מצוה pushes aside a prohibition only when you cannot keep both. Since fake dye could be caught by testing, the גמרא switches to a new reason: dye used for testing the color (טעימה) is invalid. Sending letters to warn people is rejected as unreliable. The amud ends as רבא begins a new statement that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Does a linen sheet need ציצית?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא brings a מחלוקת: בית שמאי exempt a linen סדין from ציצית, בית הלל obligate it, and the הלכה follows בית הלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: about a linen sheet and ציצית, בית שמאי say it is exempt and בית הלל say it is obligated. The הלכה follows בית הלל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא about whether a linen garment needs ציצית. בית שמאי say no, בית הלל say yes, and we follow בית הלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is that the תכלת strings are made of wool, and wool sewn onto linen is normally forbidden as שעטנז. בית שמאי therefore exempt a linen garment. בית הלל say the מצוה of ציצית overrides that problem, so the garment is obligated.

keyTerms.meaning: A sheet or cloak made of linen
The fringes tied on the corners of a four-cornered garment
They exempt (there is no obligation)
They obligate (it must have the fringes)
The final law follows the opinion of...

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think a linen garment has no connection to ציצית. According to בית הלל it truly is obligated. The steps that follow only discuss a practical decree about how people should act.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
A linen sheet, regarding tzitzit —
phrases.notes: The issue is that the תכלת strings are wool, and wool together with linen is שעטנז.

phrases.english: Beit Shammai exempt it
and Beit Hillel obligate it,
and the halacha follows the words of Beit Hillel.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A linen garment is obligated in ציצית (with wool תכלת), following בית הלל.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic law. Everything that follows explains why actual practice did not match it.

steps.title: In Jerusalem, people found it strange
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בן רבי צדוק points out that in ירושלים, anyone who put תכלת on a linen garment was seen as someone doing something strange.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן רבי צדוק said: But isn't it true that anyone who put תכלת on linen in ירושלים was treated as one of the people who make others stare in surprise?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר בן רבי צדוק raises a difficulty with the ruling. If the הלכה follows בית הלל, why did people in ירושלים think it was strange to do this?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Real practice in ירושלים seems to go against the ruling. People did not put wool תכלת on linen, and anyone who did was looked at with surprise. This suggests something was holding people back, and the next step explains what.

keyTerms.meaning: One who puts or attaches
The sky-blue wool string of ציצית
People whose actions make others surprised or puzzled

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן רַבִּי צָדוֹק:
phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok said:
But isn't it so that anyone who puts techeiles (on a linen garment) in Jerusalem
is considered nothing but one of those who cause astonishment!
phrases.notes: People would stare, because it looked like he was wearing שעטנז.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Points out that real practice in ירושלים seems to clash with the ruling of בית הלל
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the הלכה follows בית הלל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a linen garment truly needs wool תכלת, people doing it should not be seen as odd.

steps.title: The Sages forbade it because people are not experts
steps.stepSummary: רבי explains that even though the law follows בית הלל, the Sages forbade it, because ordinary people don't know the rules well.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי said: If so, why did they forbid it? Because people are not experts.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי explains the contradiction. By Torah law it is allowed, but the Sages made a decree against it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wool on linen is allowed only because of the מצוה of ציצית. People who don't know the details might think wool with linen is fine in general and come to wear real שעטנז. To prevent that mistake, the Sages forbade putting תכלת on linen.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if the law really follows בית הלל)
They (the Sages) forbade it
Experts, people who know the law well

steps.whatToRemember: A linen garment is obligated in ציצית by Torah law, but the Sages forbade putting wool תכלת on it so people would not get confused about שעטנז.

phrases.english: Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) said:
If so, why did they forbid it?
phrases.notes: "If so" means if the law really follows בית הלל and it is allowed.

phrases.english: Because people are not experts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why practice in ירושלים differed from the ruling of בית הלל
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rabbinic decree: allowed by Torah law but forbidden by the Sages
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the law follows בית הלל, it seems people should openly put תכלת on linen.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Sages forbade it because people who don't know the law might come to wear real שעטנז.

steps.title: Why not publicize that it's allowed?
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב חנא asks רבא: let ten people wear it in the marketplace so everyone learns it is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר רב חנא said to רבא: Let ten people put it on and go out to the marketplace, and the matter will become known!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר רב חנא challenges the reason for the decree. If the worry is that people don't know the law, just teach them in public.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The decree is based on people not being experts. If a group of ten went out wearing linen garments with תכלת, everyone would learn that it is allowed only for ציצית. Then the worry would be gone and the decree would not be needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Let them put on (wear)
A group of ten people
The marketplace
The matter becomes publicly known

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא בַּר רַב חָנָא לְרָבָא:
phrases.english: Rava bar Rav Chana said to Rava:
Then let ten people put them on
and go out to the marketplace
and the matter will become publicized!
phrases.notes: The word in round brackets is in some versions; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Either way it means "the matter."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי's reason for the decree
steps.kashyaTarget: The decree based on people not being experts
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If ignorance is the problem, publicizing the law fixes it, so there is no need to forbid it.

steps.title: Publicizing would only make it look stranger
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that if they did that, people would be even more surprised at them.
steps.simpleTranslation: All the more so they would be astonished at us.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge. Going out in public would not teach people. It would just make them stare even more.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ten people walking around in what looks like שעטנז would not explain the law to anyone. It would only look more shocking, so the decree stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: All the more so
That they would be astonished
At us

steps.whatToRemember: The decree against תכלת on linen stands. Publicizing it would not help, because people would only find it stranger.

phrases.english: All the more so they would be astonished at us.
phrases.notes: This is רבא answering, even though the גמרא doesn't say his name again.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion to publicize the law
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical rejection: the suggested fix would backfire
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Public wearing by ten people would teach everyone the law.
steps.terutzMaskana: People would only be more surprised, so the decree remains.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Wool תכלת is not put on linen garments, because of the Sages' decree.

steps.title: Why not teach it in a public lecture?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the Sages could simply announce in their public lecture that wool ציצית on linen is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let them teach it in the public lecture!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes again. If people would wrongly think it is forbidden, why not just teach the rule openly in the public lecture?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 5, רבא said that ten people wearing it in the market would only make people more surprised. A public lecture seems like a cleaner way to teach the הלכה to everyone, so the question is why the Sages didn't do that.

keyTerms.meaning: The public lecture given by a sage to the community, often on שבת or יום טוב
Let them teach it / expound it publicly

phrases.english: Let them teach it in the public lecture!
phrases.notes: "It" means the rule that wool ציצית on a linen garment is allowed, like בית הלל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the idea of ten people in the market is rejected, the גמרא offers a different way to spread the הלכה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the Sages had to forbid it because ordinary people don't know the rules.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the only problem is that people don't know the rule, teaching it publicly would fix that, so there is no need for a ban.

steps.title: A decree because of fake blue dye
steps.stepSummary: The ban is a גזירה because people might use strings dyed with קלא אילן, a fake blue, instead of real תכלת.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a decree because of indigo (fake blue dye).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the real problem isn't only ignorance. It is a גזירה, because people might use fake blue dye.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wool ציצית on linen is only allowed because the מצוה of ציצית pushes aside the ban on כלאים. If the blue strings are really dyed with קלא אילן and not real תכלת, there is no מצוה of תכלת, and the person ends up wearing כלאים for nothing. A public lecture can't stop people from buying fake dye.

keyTerms.meaning: A protective decree of the Sages, made to keep people from coming to break a Torah law
Indigo, a plant dye that looks like תכלת but is not valid for the מצוה
Here: the Torah ban on wearing wool and linen together (שעטנז)

steps.confusionAlert: The problem isn't that קלא אילן is just a less nice color. Without real תכלת there may be no מצוה to push aside כלאים, so wearing wool on linen could become a real Torah transgression.

phrases.english: It is a decree because of indigo.
phrases.notes: Indigo looks just like real תכלת, so people could easily be fooled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 6 by showing the ban has a deeper reason that a lecture can't solve.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a new reason: a protective decree, not just ignorance of the law.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The only problem is that people don't know the הלכה, so teaching it would solve everything.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Sages made a גזירה because of the danger of fake blue dye, which would leave a person wearing כלאים without a real מצוה.

steps.title: Let fake-blue strings count as white
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues that even strings dyed with קלא אילן should at least count as white strings, which are still valid ציצית.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it be no worse than white!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer in Step 7. Even if the blue is fake, the strings should still count as ordinary white ציצית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person keeps the מצוה of ציצית even with only white strings. So even with fake blue there is still a real מצוה, and that מצוה should push aside כלאים. If so, the danger of קלא אילן doesn't seem to matter.

keyTerms.meaning: White: the plain, undyed strings of ציצית
Let it be no worse than: at the very least, treat it as

phrases.english: Let it be no worse than white!
phrases.notes: He means: treat the fake-blue string like a plain white one, which still counts for the מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason given in Step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The decree because of קלא אילן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Fake-blue strings still work as white strings, so there is still a מצוה that can push aside כלאים. The fear of fake dye shouldn't cause any real problem.

steps.title: Linen strings are possible, so wool is not allowed
steps.stepSummary: Since one can make white strings from linen, the same material as the garment, there is no need to use wool and push aside כלאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since it is possible with their own kind, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that white strings don't need to be wool. A linen garment can get white linen strings, so wool white strings are not allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only reason to use wool on linen is the תכלת, which must be wool. If the blue is fake and only counts as white, then the מצוה could have been done with linen strings and no כלאים at all. So the מצוה does not push aside כלאים here.

keyTerms.meaning: Possible: there is another way to do it
With their own kind: strings made of the same material as the garment (here, linen)

phrases.english: Since it is possible with their own kind, no.
phrases.notes: "Their own kind" means linen strings for a linen garment, so no wool and no כלאים are needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 8 and so defends the decree of Step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits when a מצוה can push aside a prohibition: only when there is no other way.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any valid מצוה of ציצית, even with only white strings, pushes aside כלאים.
steps.terutzMaskana: White strings can be linen, so wool white strings on linen are still כלאים. The decree because of קלא אילן stands.

steps.title: ריש לקיש's rule: keep both if you can
steps.stepSummary: The answer matches ריש לקיש's principle: when an עשה and a לא תעשה clash, keep both if possible; only if not does the עשה push aside the לא תעשה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This follows ריש לקיש, who said: whenever you find a positive מצוה and a prohibition clashing, if you can keep both, that is best. If not, the positive מצוה comes and pushes aside the prohibition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that its answer in Step 9 is based on a known rule of ריש לקיש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עשה דוחה לא תעשה is not a free pass. If there is a way to keep both the מצוה and the prohibition, you must use it. Here, linen white strings keep both ציצית and the ban on כלאים, so wool may not be used.

keyTerms.meaning: A positive מצוה: something the Torah commands you to do
A prohibition: something the Torah forbids
A positive מצוה overrides a prohibition
Best / preferable

steps.whatToRemember: A positive מצוה only pushes aside a prohibition when there is no way to keep both. If a way exists, you must take it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule of ריש לקיש is used all over the Torah whenever a מצוה and a prohibition seem to clash. It explains why white wool strings on linen are not allowed.

phrases.english: This is like ריש לקיש,
as ריש לקיש said:
Any place where you find
a positive מצוה and a prohibition,
phrases.notes: He means the two clash, so doing one seems to break the other.

phrases.aramaic: אִם אַתָּה יָכוֹל לְקַיֵּים אֶת שְׁנֵיהֶם – מוּטָב,
phrases.english: if you are able to keep both of them, that is best,
and if not,

phrases.aramaic: יָבוֹא עֲשֵׂה וְיִדְחֶה אֶת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה.
phrases.english: the positive מצוה shall come and push aside the prohibition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the general rule behind the answer in Step 9.
steps.raayaObject: The answer that wool white strings are not allowed on linen, since linen strings are possible.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ריש לקיש's general rule about an עשה clashing with a לא תעשה.

steps.title: Why not test the dye?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests testing the blue strings to find out whether they are real תכלת or קלא אילן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the decree of Step 7 again. If the worry is fake dye, just check the strings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are ways to test whether blue dye is real תכלת or קלא אילן. If a test can catch the fake, the danger of קלא אילן goes away, and so does the reason for the decree.

keyTerms.meaning: Let them test it: check the dye to see if it is real

phrases.english: Let them test it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the decree of קלא אילן from Step 7 and attacks it from a new angle.
steps.kashyaTarget: The decree because of קלא אילן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Fake dye can be found out by testing, so there's no need to ban ציצית on linen.

steps.title: The real reason: dye used for testing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes its reason: the decree is because of טעימה, תכלת dye that was used to test the color and so became invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is a decree because of the testing dye.
steps.whatsHappening: The word "rather" tells us the גמרא is giving a new reason for the decree. The worry is תכלת that was used for testing the dye, which is not valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dye used to test the color in the vat (טעימה) becomes unfit for ציצית, as explained on 42b. So the strings would have no valid תכלת and no מצוה to push aside כלאים. A color test can't catch this, because it was still real תכלת dye.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally "tasting": תכלת dye used to test the color, which makes it unfit for the מצוה
Rather: signals a change to a new explanation

steps.whatToRemember: The Sages banned ציצית on linen even though הלכה follows בית הלל. The reason the גמרא now settles on is a גזירה because of טעימה: invalid תכלת would mean wearing כלאים with no מצוה to allow it.

phrases.english: Rather, it is a decree because of the testing dye.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the point of Step 11 and replaces the reason from Step 7 with a new one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replaces the earlier reason with a new reason that testing can't solve.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The decree is because of קלא אילן, which a test could catch.
steps.terutzMaskana: The decree is because of טעימה: dye used for testing is invalid, so there would be no מצוה to push aside כלאים.

steps.title: Why not just send letters warning about the test dye?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the חכמים could simply write letters warning people that טעימה dye is not valid, instead of forbidding wool ציצית on linen altogether.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the decree based on טעימה. If the only worry is that people will use test dye, why not just send out letters telling everyone that this dye is not valid?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The decree from step 12 is a broad ban: no wool ציצית on linen at all. The challenge says a narrower fix exists, which is to inform people so they avoid the test dye. If a simple warning works, a sweeping גזירה seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: Letters or written notices sent out to inform people
Let them write it (a suggestion: 'why not just write?')

phrases.english: Let them write letters!
phrases.notes: The idea is to send out notices telling people that dye used for testing the color is not valid for ציצית.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the decree based on טעימה that step 12 introduced.
steps.kashyaTarget: The decree forbidding wool ציצית on a linen garment because of טעימה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A simpler, narrower solution (written warnings) would handle the problem, so a sweeping ban seems unnecessary.

steps.title: We cannot rely on letters
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that letters are not reliable enough to depend on, so the decree is still needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should we go and rely on letters?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion with a rhetorical question: are we really going to depend on letters? The point is no, we cannot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Letters might not reach everyone, and people who get them might not follow them. Since the warning cannot be trusted to work, the חכמים needed a firm decree instead. The decree based on טעימה stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we get up, go ahead (and do something)
And rely on, depend on

steps.confusionAlert: This line looks like a question, but it is really the answer. It means 'Can we rely on letters? Of course not!'

phrases.english: Shall we go and rely on letters?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 13 and defends the decree from step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical rejection: the suggested alternative is not reliable
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Sending letters could replace the decree.
steps.terutzMaskana: Letters cannot be relied on, so the decree about טעימה is needed.
steps.whatToRemember: The ban on wool ציצית for a linen garment rests on the worry about טעימה, and a simple written warning was not considered enough to prevent it.

steps.title: רבא begins a new comment
steps.stepSummary: רבא starts a new statement with the word 'now'. The rest of his statement continues in the next section.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move: רבא begins speaking with 'now', building on what was just established. His full point comes in the following text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word הַשְׁתָּא often opens an argument of the form 'now, if this is so…'. רבא's sentence breaks off here, so we cannot yet tell whether he is backing the answer about letters or challenging it. The rest of his statement continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Now; often means 'now that we have established this'

phrases.english: Rava said: Now,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new comment by רבא following the discussion of the decree; its content continues on the next amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Incomplete here; רבא's statement continues in the next section.
